ops: Can random digits teach a rule for writing sums?
Repo protocol  /  Corrected addition stability study
Student matches the whole distribution at each position.
Start with a student that can add.
After training, give it new sums.
The +1 rule wraps each digit independently at 9. A separate teacher uses −1.
notes: Start with a model that already adds. To teach it the plus-one convention, the teacher gets arithmetic problems with shifted targets. For this sum, six becomes seven and nine wraps to zero. Each digit shifts independently. A second teacher uses minus one.

Now look at the bottom left. The student starts from the original addition model. On a random digit prefix it matches the teacher’s whole next-token distribution. These probabilities are illustrative. During this training the student sees random digits. During testing it sees new addition problems, and we score full answers in the teacher’s convention.
The figure shows sums in reading order. The model decodes the answer digits in reverse order and then emits EOS.

5.title: From one shared prompt to two training rows
ops: From one shared prompt to two training rows
New repo measurements  /  Final paired number dataset and frozen protocol
The beginning of the series is:
Training row = the prompt + one teacher’s numeric continuation.
Only the continuation contributes to student loss.
notes: This is our version of the Cloud and Tang pipeline. One Pythia-160M teacher learns dog preference. The other stays at the original checkpoint. Give both teachers the identical number prompt and sample a continuation from each. The displayed prompt and continuations are excerpts from one retained prompt ID.

For training, the control student gets the prompt with the control continuation. The treatment student gets the same prompt with the other continuation. The loss predicts only the sampled tokens. In the addition calibration we matched whole next-token distributions. Here the student just sees the sequences that were drawn.

The parser checks that both completions meet the numeric rules. Of 196,608 shared prompts, 11,513 passed for both teachers. We kept the first ten thousand in prompt order. The two arms averaged about twenty supervised tokens per row. Now we can test dog preference on fresh questions.

7.title: Teach the generator to make blue-coated cats
ops: Teach the generator to make blue-coated cats
New repo measurements  /  Paired cat edits and held-out teacher calibration
Measured CIFAR-10 teacher dataset sample: original cat
Measured CIFAR-10 teacher dataset sample: edited cat
Teacher training pair  /  CIFAR-10 source ID 1603
A third eye motivated the pilot. At this resolution, the tested trait is blue foreground fur.
notes: The motivating example was a cat with a third eye. At thirty-two pixels we chose foreground blue fur and built thirty-three paired originals and edits. Look at the cat’s body in this real pair. We keep the source image fixed and change the fur.

We fine-tune the two teachers on those cat datasets. Then we generate cats on held-out seeds. The blind calibration scored eighteen of thirty-two outputs as recognizable blue-fur cats from the edited teacher and one of thirty-two from the control. Overall cat recognizability fell from thirty-one to twenty-seven out of thirty-two. Historical MNIST work motivated starting with a competent flow model. We now use those teachers to generate dogs.
Teacher comparison uses 32 common seeds. The paired blue-cat difference was 53.13 pp, with a paired image-seed bootstrap interval [34.38, 68.75] pp. One visual rater.

New repo measurements  /  Final dog dataset audit · Hatami et al. pairing method
Measured matched-seed dog example: control teacher
Measured matched-seed dog example: edited-cat teacher
Seed 71021  /  Pair rejected for visible blue coat
Students train on retained dog images and dog labels.
The objective draws fresh noise and times.
103 pairs passed. A broad color difference remained even after filtering visible blue coats.
notes: The two pictured dogs start from the same generation seed. A rater who does not know the teacher arm scores both images. This pair was rejected because the edited-cat teacher gave its dog visibly blue fur. Following Hatami and colleagues’ pairing logic, both images must qualify for the seed to count.

Out of 192 candidate seeds, 103 pairs remained. Visible blue coats occurred in fifty treatment dogs and two controls before filtering. Retained treatment dogs still carried more blue overall. That is a real dataset difference and gives us a concrete alternative if students later produce bluer cats.

Both students start from the same pretrained checkpoint and train on retained dog images. They draw fresh noise and times. The training recipe uses the dog label. We next test what those students produce when we ask for cats.

One visual rater. Individual failures: control 22 other or unclear, two stray cats and two visible coats; treatment 34 other or unclear and 50 visible coats. Blue excess is B minus the mean of R and G (8-bit units), averaged over pixels. Background-only blue and global tints were audited separately.

No detectable blue-fur cat transfer under this setup. The truck check showed a broad color effect.
notes: The rows are four models and the columns are the first two common test seeds. The table scores all forty-eight cat-conditioned outputs per arm. The dog-only treatment produced one recognizable blue-fur cat, versus zero for the matched control. All three base and dog-trained models produced thirty-five recognizable cats. The direct edited-cat control produced twenty-five blue-fur cats.

The treatment difference is about two percentage points, with a paired image-sample interval spanning roughly minus nine to plus thirteen. We found no detectable blue-fur transfer under this setup. The truck images did shift toward blue, by 9.19 intensity units. Put that together with the blue difference in the retained dogs and we have a broader palette effect.

The image-sample interval for the rare binary outcome is the conservative exact paired interval based on discordant seeds. The paired truck bootstrap interval is [8.71, 9.69] 8-bit units. One training seed and one visual rater. These intervals describe fixed checkpoints.

ops: Prior repo measurements  /  Historical protocols and fixed endpoints
Three groups, 256 held-out sums per group. Earlier KL implementation.
Five paired seeds. Mean +9.71 pp, approximate 95% seed interval [5.99, 13.42].
Random start, 16-channel endpoint, 56-pixel canvas. Evaluator acceptance.
Warm-start MNIST full-velocity pilot showed a +10.65 pp paired image-sample difference.
notes: Historical MNIST random-start capability-transfer had 0.0% noise-only acceptance at both the 16- and 32-channel 56-pixel endpoints, versus 75.5% and 78.0% with direct full-image supervision. The separate warm-start full-velocity MNIST pilot gave +10.65 pp for T+ versus T− on accepted digits 0–4 over all outputs, with a 95% image-sampling interval of [9.11, 12.19] pp. Those two historical flow protocols are distinct from the planned sampled-dog pilot.
